strengths: Clear and well-motivated reformulation of VLA policy learning as a POMDP, addressing a real limitation (history-agnostic, per-frame processing) in current VLA architectures such as OpenVLA-OFT.

The proposed Active Visual Attention (AVA) module and recurrent-state mechanism are technically sound and reasonably simple to integrate into an existing parallel-decoding VLA backbone (cross-attention between visual tokens and a recurrent state, soft weighting of attention masks).

Broad and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation: LIBERO (both single-suite and multi-suite settings), CALVIN ABC->D, LIBERO+ perturbation robustness benchmark, and real-world dual-arm Mobile ALOHA experiments across four diverse manipulation tasks, with consistent improvements over strong recent baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, UniVLA, FLOWER, RIPT-VLA, etc.).

Ablations are informative: backbone-agnostic gains (OpenVLA-7B, LLaMA2-7B, Qwen2.5-0.5B), decomposition of AVA module vs. state-based initialization, and an interesting byproduct application to visual token pruning showing minimal performance loss even at 70-90% token reduction.

Qualitative visualizations (soft-weight heatmaps) across many tasks and viewpoints (main paper and appendix) provide reasonably convincing evidence that the module attends to task-relevant regions (gripper, target objects) rather than being just a black-box gain.
Good coverage of related work distinguishing this POMDP-based active attention approach from existing token-pruning/efficiency-focused works and from passive-history VLM methods.
weaknesses: The magnitude of improvement over the strongest baseline (OpenVLA-OFT) is often small (e.g., LIBERO average SR 98.0 vs 97.6, or 98.3 vs 96.9), raising questions about statistical significance given no reported variance/seeds/multiple runs across benchmarks.

The claimed novelty of using a 'recurrent state' as a belief-state approximation is conceptually similar to standard recurrent/history-conditioning approaches in RL and prior VLA/robot-learning work (e.g., RNN policies, KV-cache reuse referenced in related work); the POMDP framing is a nice narrative but the core mechanism (cross-attention to a persistent hidden vector) is an incremental architectural addition rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

Truncated BPTT with a short horizon (T=4) is used due to compute constraints; the paper does not analyze how sensitive results are to this truncation length or whether longer temporal context would yield further gains, limiting insight into the true benefit of the belief-state formulation versus a fixed short window of history.

The real-world evaluation, while appreciated, uses small trial counts (24-30 trials per task) and compares against only two baselines (UniVLA, OpenVLA-OFT), which limits generalizability of real-robot claims; no statistical analysis (e.g., confidence intervals) is provided for these small-sample results.

The regularization loss (Eq. 13) forcing the mean soft weight toward a fixed target c is a somewhat ad hoc design choice; the paper does not fully justify why this constraint is necessary or analyze its sensitivity, nor does it explore alternative regularization strategies.

Figures with attention/soft-weight visualizations (e.g., Fig. 5-10) are qualitative anecdotes on cherry-picked frames; no quantitative metric (e.g., IoU with task-relevant regions, correlation with object bounding boxes) is provided to substantiate the interpretability claims objectively.

The method is tied specifically to parallel-decoding, chunked-action VLA models (like OpenVLA-OFT); it's unclear how the approach would extend to autoregressive VLA architectures or diffusion-based action heads, limiting the generality of the contribution despite claims about improving 'VLA models' broadly.

strengths: Well-motivated reformulation of VLA policy learning from an MDP to a POMDP perspective, providing a principled theoretical lens for why history-agnostic visual processing is suboptimal.

The Active Visual Attention (AVA) module is a clean, lightweight addition (cross-attention between current visual tokens and a recurrent 'belief' state) that is architecture-agnostic and can be layered on different VLA backbones (demonstrated on OpenVLA-7B, LLaMA2-7B, Qwen2.5-0.5B backbones in Table 3).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning LIBERO (single-task and multi-task settings), CALVIN ABC→D, the LIBERO+ robustness benchmark with 7 perturbation types, and real-world Mobile ALOHA dual-arm experiments across 4 diverse task suites, with consistent state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance.

Useful ablations isolating the contributions of the AVA module vs. state-based placeholder initialization (Table 4), and a practical exploration of using the learned soft weights for visual token pruning (Table 5), showing the learned attention scores are meaningful and have a secondary efficiency benefit.

Good qualitative visualizations (Figures 5-10) across simulation and real-world tasks showing the attention consistently localizes to contact regions and task-relevant objects, supporting the claimed interpretability and effectiveness of the module.
Reasonably detailed implementation and appendix documentation (training hyperparameters, task suite descriptions, real-robot setup), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Many of the reported gains over the strong OpenVLA-OFT baseline are numerically small (e.g., LIBERO average SR 96.8→98.0 or 97.1→97.5, CALVIN improvements of a few points), and no variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for simulation or real-world trials, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the improvements.

The 'belief state' framing is more of an inspirational analogy than a formally grounded POMDP solution; the recurrent state is simply an MLP-transformed hidden state from the previous timestep, conceptually similar to prior recurrent-history conditioning approaches (e.g., RNN/LSTM policies), and the paper does not compare against a simpler recurrent-history baseline (e.g., naive frame history concatenation or an LSTM-based state encoder without the attention/FiLM machinery) to isolate how much of the gain comes specifically from the 'active' attention mechanism versus merely adding recurrence.

Truncated BPTT is used with a short horizon (T=4) and gradients are detached between the second and third timestep without clear justification or ablation of this design choice, which could limit the model's ability to capture genuinely long-horizon dependencies despite the long-horizon motivation of the paper.

Real-world experiments only compare against two baselines (UniVLA and OpenVLA-OFT), a much narrower comparison than the simulation benchmarks, and use small trial counts (24-30 trials per task) without repeated runs, limiting confidence in the real-robot claims.

The loss regularization target mean c for the soft weights differs between benchmarks (0.6 for LIBERO vs. 0.2 for CALVIN) without a principled explanation, suggesting sensitivity to this hyperparameter that is not analyzed.

Added architectural complexity (multiple MLPs, FiLM conditioning, cross-attention, modified attention masking across all LLM layers) is not accompanied by a computational overhead/latency/memory comparison against the baseline OpenVLA-OFT, despite claims of efficiency being touted as a byproduct benefit.

strengths: Well-motivated reformulation of VLA policy learning from an MDP to a POMDP perspective, providing a principled theoretical grounding for introducing history-awareness via a recurrent state rather than an ad hoc engineering fix.

The Active Visual Attention (AVA) module is a lightweight (<1% parameter overhead) and architecturally clean mechanism that modulates visual token importance using both instruction and recurrent historical context, and is compatible with parallel-decoding VLA backbones like OpenVLA-OFT.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world dual-arm Mobile ALOHA tasks, with consistent state-of-the-art or competitive performance against many recent strong baselines (UnifiedVLA, FLOWER, RIPT-VLA, pi0-FAST, etc.).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of state-based initialization vs. the AVA module, backbone generalization (OpenVLA-7B, LLaMA2-7B, Qwen2.5-0.5B), the L2 regularizer, and robustness under matched training compute (Appendix D.1), which helps rule out the possibility that gains stem merely from extra training rather than the proposed mechanism.

Additional robustness evaluation on the LIBERO+ perturbation benchmark (camera, lighting, background, noise, layout) showing meaningful average gains, supporting generalization claims beyond curated benchmark conditions.

Interpretability analysis (qualitative attention visualizations across multiple tasks/viewpoints, Figures 4danger, 7–12) that plausibly demonstrates the model's attention concentrates on task-relevant regions (gripper, target object) over time, and an honest discussion of failure cases and limitations (belief drift in long-horizon/precision tasks).
weaknesses: The 'recurrent state' is derived only from the immediately preceding timestep's hidden state (r^{t-1} computed from h_M^{t-1}), which is itself computed without explicit backprop through longer history beyond truncated BPTT with T=4; the claim of capturing a POMDP belief over the full trajectory is not strongly substantiated versus a simple short-window recency mechanism, and the theoretical POMDP framing may overstate what is actually implemented.

No comparison to simpler, cheaper baselines that also incorporate short historical context (e.g., naive frame concatenation, stacking last K frames, or a simple temporal attention/LSTM over raw features) to isolate whether the gains come specifically from the proposed active/soft-weighting mechanism versus simply adding any historical signal.

Ablation studies (Table 4) show relatively modest and sometimes non-monotonic improvements from AVA/state-init individually (e.g., AVA module alone sometimes ties or slightly underperforms OpenVLA-OFT on Spatial/Object SR), raising questions about how robust/necessary each component is outside the aggregate metric; variance/multiple-seed reporting is absent throughout, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the (often <1-2%) gains over strong baselines like OpenVLA-OFT.

Real-world Mobile ALOHA evaluation is limited to a single robot platform, a small number of tasks (4) and modest trial counts (24-30 per task), with comparison only against two baselines (UniVLA, OpenVLA-OFT), limiting generalizability claims for real-world transfer.

The failure case analysis (Figure 13) reveals that belief drift over long horizons can degrade precision-sensitive tasks, which is an acknowledged core limitation of the POMDP/recurrent-state approach, but no mitigation or quantitative analysis of how often/severely this occurs is provided.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation (Eqs. 1-14) that could be streamlined; some architectural design choices (e.g., specific choice of FiLM conditioning, cross-attention with recurrent state as K/V rather than Q) are not ablated individually, making it unclear which specific architectural decisions within AVA are most responsible for the gains.

strengths: Clear theoretical motivation: reformulating VLA policy learning from an MDP to a POMDP perspective is a sensible and underexplored framing that explains a concrete limitation of frame-independent VLA processing.

The proposed recurrent-state + Active Visual Attention (AVA) mechanism is lightweight (<50M added parameters, <1% of backbone size) yet is evaluated extensively across three simulation/real-world settings (LIBERO, CALVIN, Mobile ALOHA), achieving state-of-the-art or highly competitive results in most settings.

Thorough ablation studies: backbone generalization (OpenVLA-7B, LLaMA2-7B, Qwen2.5-0.5B), decomposition of the two components (state-based init vs. AVA module), loss regularizer effect, matched-training-compute comparison (Appendix D.1), and module ablation on CALVIN — these collectively make a reasonably convincing case that gains are not simply due to extra parameters or training compute.

Good qualitative analysis: soft-weight visualizations (Fig. 4, 7-11) show visual attention concentrating on task-relevant regions (gripper contact points, target objects) and comparison with OpenVLA-OFT baseline (Fig. 1) supports the claim of more stable/task-relevant focus.

Honest limitations section with concrete failure-case visualizations (Fig. 13) discussing belief drift in long-horizon, precision-sensitive tasks, which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.
A useful side application (visual token pruning) is explored, showing the learned soft weights are informative beyond action prediction, with minimal performance degradation up to 70% pruning.
weaknesses: The performance gains on the main LIBERO benchmark are often numerically small (e.g., 98.0% vs. 97.6% average SR for OpenVLA-OFT in the multi-suite setting; 97.5% vs. 97.5% in the module-only ablation), since the baseline is already near ceiling; the practical significance of these gains is not deeply discussed (e.g., no statistical significance testing or variance across seeds/trials is reported).

In the isolated-component ablation (Table 4), the AVA module alone and state-based initialization alone yield nearly identical average SR (97.5% each), and the AVA module alone actually underperforms OpenVLA-OFT on Long SR (96.6% vs 95.3% baseline improved marginally) — this makes it harder to attribute the paper's central contribution (active visual attention) to a large, unambiguous improvement independent of the simpler initialization trick.

Robustness results on LIBERO+ (Table 6, Appendix D.3) are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: AVA-VLA is not the best method on several individual perturbation types (e.g., Camera and Robot perturbations, where π0-FAST or π0 outperform it), with the method's advantage concentrated in Light/Background/Layout/Noise columns and the average driven mainly by strong performance on a subset of dimensions.

No direct empirical comparison to other explicitly history/memory-aware VLA baselines (e.g., MemoryVLA, cited and discussed conceptually in Appendix C but not benchmarked quantitatively), which would better substantiate the specific advantage of the proposed POMDP/recurrent-state formulation over alternative memory mechanisms.

Truncated BPTT is limited to a short horizon (T=4), and the method still exhibits belief drift and degraded performance on long-horizon, precision-sensitive tasks (LIBERO-Long, real-world moka-pot grasping failure in Fig. 13); the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this core limitation, leaving open whether the recurrent state genuinely captures long-range temporal dependencies as motivated in the introduction.

Real-world evaluation is limited in scale (4 tasks, 24-30 trials each, single robot platform/embodiment) and baselines are restricted to only two methods (UniVLA, OpenVLA-OFT), which constrains generalizability claims about real-world applicability.
